items.title: Nuggets Notes: Watson, Walker, Contract, Strawther
items.content:
The Nuggets continue to discuss potential Peyton Watson sign-and-trade scenarios with multiple teams, according to ESPN’s Shams Charania, who reports that Denver is in “active talks” with those rival clubs.

Charania specifically lists the Cavaliers, Bucks and Clippers as three of the teams pursuing the restricted free agent forward. All three clubs have been previously linked to Watson.

Although it’s long been assumed that Denver’s preference would be to retain Watson, the two sides reportedly have a gap in perceived valuation on his next deal. The Nuggets are said to be offering something in the $16-18MM range, whereas Watson is hoping for a more lucrative contract.

Here’s more on the Nuggets:

Charania’s report about Watson was a bookend to his Sunday night story about Lonnie Walker IV agreeing to a one-year deal with Denver. According to Bennett Durando of The Denver Post (Twitter link), the veteran guard will be signing a non-guaranteed training camp deal with the Nuggets and will be competing for a roster spot. While Walker will occupy a roster spot either way once the deal is official, there are a few notable difference between a training camp deal and a typical non-guaranteed standard contract.
As Luke Adams explained yesterday in updated our glossary entry on Exhibit 9 agreements, an Exhibit 9 clause protects an NBA team in the event that a player suffers a significant injury in training camp. If a player on a standard non-guaranteed contract without an Exhibit 9 clause suffered such an injury, his club would be required to pay him his salary until he’s healthy enough to play or until the end of that season, whichever comes first. If the injured player’s contract includes Exhibit 9 language, however, his team could waive him and only be on the hook for a one-time payment of $15K.
Exhibit 9 contracts also don’t count against the salary cap, which is an important consideration for the Nuggets, who are currently the only NBA team over the second tax apron. If Walker makes the team out of camp, his Exhibit 9 deal would be converted into a typical non-guaranteed contract. The Exhibit 9 protection wouldn’t carry over into the regular season.
Reacting to the news of Walker’s signing, Harrison Wind and Adam Mares of DNVR Sports (YouTube link) wondered how the 27-year-old’s addition would impact former first-round pick Julian Strawther, who’s eligible this offseason for a rookie scale extension. Strawther’s points and minutes per game decreased from 2024/25 to 2025/26 in part because he was outplayed by veteran wing Tim Hardaway Jr., who signed with Miami this summer. Strawther, 24, will be a restricted free agent in 2027 if he doesn’t sign an extension.

items.title: Anthony Davis, Wizards to reportedly hold off contract extension talks until after 2026-27 NBA season begins
items.content:
If Anthony Davis and the Washington Wizards reach agreement on a contract extension, it won't happen until during the 2026-27 NBA season.

Davis and the Wizards have mutually decided to hold off talks on an extension until at least 20 games into the season, The Athletic's Josh Robbins reports. The 14-year NBA veteran became eligible to sign an extension of up to four years and $275 million on Thursday. 

The two sides will wait to see how they fit together with a new roster that includes 2026 No. 1 overall pick AJ Dybantsa; center Deandre Ayton, acquired from the Los Angeles Lakers; and point guard Trae Young, who signed a four-year, $212 million extension with Washington in July. 

Reporting for NBA Today on the Wizards and Anthony Davis deciding to wait until the regular season to navigate a potential contract extension: pic.twitter.com/9PRGnoujQe

— Shams Charania (@ShamsCharania) August 6, 2026If Davis, 33, signs an extension with the Wizards, the first year of the new deal would replace the $62.8 player option that he currently holds for the 2027-28 season. He is set to be paid $58.5 million in the final year of the three-year, $175 million max extension he signed with the Lakers in August 2023. 

Davis was traded to the Wizards from the Dallas Mavericks in February as part of an eight-player deal. However, the 6-foot-10 forward never took the court for Washington due to hand and finger injuries. He only played 20 games in total last season, averaging 20.4 points, 11.1 rebounds, 2.8 assists, 1.1 steals and 1.7 blocks. 

That history of injuries likely has the Wizards reluctant to commit to a multiyear extension. Since playing a career-high 76 games during the 2023-24 campaign, Davis has played 71 games in total across the past two seasons. Only three times during his 14 NBA seasons has he played in at least 75 games. But he has career averages of 24.0 points, 10.7 rebounds and 2.3 blocks per contest.

Davis may also be hesitant to sign long-term with a Wizards team that finished with the NBA's worst record last year at 17-65 — albeit without Davis and Young while tanking in an attempt to win the NBA Draft Lottery and the No. 1 overall selection. 

Washington has won fewer than 20 games for the past three seasons and hasn't won 40 or more games since the 2017-18 campaign. (The Wizards did make the playoffs during the COVID-shortened 2020-21 season with a 34-38 record.) 

However, Davis has expressed optimism about the Wizards' young talent that includes Dybantsa, center Alex Sarr, (16.3 PPG,  7.4 RPG, 2 BPG) forwards Kyshawn George (14.8 PPG), Julian Reese (10.5 PPG, 11.8 RPG) and Will Riley (10.3), and guards Tre Johnson (12.2) , Bilal Coulibaly (11.7) and Bub Carrington (10.7).
